title: No Dissent in the Climateers' Cubbyhouse
text:
No Dissent in the Climateers’ Cubbyhouse
But what if The Science is storytelling, and the independence of narrators an illusion? What if these bodies are less guardians of truth than group-chat participants reinforcing each other while excluding contrary evidence? The public imagines impartial science is guiding policy. In reality, much comes from organisations bound by shared assumptions, overlapping careers, and a conviction that debate is finished.
Australia’s climate policy is shaped by a revolving door of activists, NGOs and sympathetic politicians reinforcing each other’s narratives. The result is managed groupthink that reduces democratic accountability. Particularly troubling is the usurping of Parliament — the bedrock of democracy — by unelected bureaucracies, in effect a third tier of government. Examples include the e-Safety Commissioner, the Climate Change Authority, the Murray–Darling Basin Authority, the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, and the Net Zero Economy Authority.
Rule by NGO
The modern story begins not with scientists but with businessman-philanthropist Robert Purves. As former president of WWF Australia, Purves used his wealth to fund a new model of activism. Through his Purves Environmental Fund (PEF), a tax-deductible charity, he bankrolls campaigns, projects, and individuals who carry his messages into business, education and politics. PEF annual reports list “achievements” that are not products of debate or unambiguous science, but of targeted investments in advocacy.
One of his highest-profile beneficiaries was Professor Tim Flannery. Purves funded Flannery’s 2005 book The Weather Makers — a speculative work widely distributed through schools. He also funded Flannery to establish the Copenhagen Climate Council, which convened the 2009 World Business Summit on Climate Change. The goal was to corral business leaders behind the UN’s COP15 process. Many such leaders interact with Australian politicians and influence policy. (Many also supported the failed Voice referendum.)
The issue is not whether environmentalism is wrong, but that Purves and WWF run both sides of a storyline: the alarmist one — glossy brochures, emotive photos, crafted one-liners — and the “solution” pushed relentlessly into the public square. His Wentworth Group of Concerned Scientists engineered the Murray–Darling Basin Plan, which is a prime example.
They don’t have to show the MDB or the Reef imperilled. A few photos of long-dead trees or bleached coral, some hand-picked experts, with fingers pointed at rice-growers, cane-growers and graziers suffice. Against fire-bombed landscapes resulting from the failure of authorities to undertake pre-emptive hazard reduction, their “save the koala” campaign reinforces illusions of near-extinction without resorting to hard evidence.
But what if they also own The Science? As patron of the Lizard Island research facility off Cairns, and with WWF a major player in heritage protection, research contradicting their narratives may be downplayed, drowned out or dismissed. Could critics lose their jobs? What if, under the guise of homogenisation, the Bureau of Meteorology adjusts temperature data to support model-based narratives of climate doom that is on-sold into school curricula?
Who They Are
The Climate Council was born of politics. The Abbott government abolished the Gillard-era Climate Commission in 2013. Led by Flannery, the Commission had issued highly publicised warnings of catastrophes — none of which were unprecedented, and all of which failed to unfold. The rains returned, dams filled, snow still falls. With Purves as Director and Flannery as Chief Councillor within days the group re-formed as the privately funded Climate Council, branding itself “community supported” and “independent”.
Sponsored by Zali Stegall, herself championed by Purves, the Climate Change Authority (CCA) was set up by statute in 2012 to advise on emissions and climate policy. It simply echoes the same themes: catastrophism, net-zero urgency, renewables as destiny, and fossil fuels as stranded assets.
Membership patterns reveal the club. Professors specialising in “impacts” or “adaptation”; former CSIRO or Bureau of Meteorology people advancing narratives they helped create; lobbyists and economists whose careers hinge on climate policy and carbon trading. Absent are independent climatologists, physical scientists or geologists with a record of questioning prevailing views.
Take Professor Lesley Hughes — an ecologist whose career rests largely on modelling “what if” climate scenarios. As Climate Commissioner she co-authored The Critical Decade. Long-associated with WWF, an IPCC lead author, and Climate Council member, she contributes to inquiries and media commentary while also sitting on the CCA. What man might see as conflicting roles — professor, activist, lobbyist, adviser, grant recipient — undermine the perception of impartiality.
Following Sam Mostyn’s appointment as Governor-General, Amanda McKenzie now heads the Climate Council. With Purves’ support, she co-founded the Australian Youth Climate Coalition with activist Anna Rose. Rose is a WWF governor, co-founder of Farmers for Climate Action. Rose married former GetUp director Simon Sheikh, who runs the green super fund Future Super.
As head of the Climate Council, McKenzie engages directly with politicians, including former NSW Environment Minister and Liberal Treasurer Matt Kean. Now Chair of the CCA, Kean is a vocal proponent of green energy. These multiple hats show how entwined NGOs, activists, academics, funders and sympathetic politicians have become. They are an ecosystem – activists broadcast their message, like-minded politicians advance their careers, while others are cast aside.Democracy Subverted
Collectivists in the climate drama cannot be regarded as neutral. There is no separating the voices of activist professors, the CCA, the Climate Council, WWF, Robert Purves, and his Wentworth Group. From 11 December 2024 another authority appeared — the Net Zero Economy Authority, tasked with “helping Australia transform”, essentially by paying out displaced workers as coal plants close.
As Net Zero drives energy costs higher, opportunities for productive work in manufacturing, forestry, agriculture and mining will decline. There will be no economic boom from shutting down industries. Furthermore, pushed by globalists and WWF, primary industries and communities will come under even more pressure as environmental standards and “nature-positive” market-based solutions become legislated.
Right on cue, WWF hails yet another “independent regulator” — Environmental Protection Australia — to oversee and enforce laws it has long promoted. While it remains to be seen, expect WWF supporters and hand-picked advocates to be prominent on the list of board appointees.
The Mirage of Independence
The magic word is “independent”. The Climate Council insists it is independent because it is privately funded. But its lifeblood is donations from philanthropists with environmental agendas. Independence should mean distance from vested interests, understanding of empirical evidence, willingness to test competing explanations, and openness to uncertainty. Instead we see insiders singing from the same songbook. If a body is set up to confirm a narrative and staffed by the already convinced, the outcome is predictable. A truly independent panel would include dissenters, sceptics, and those who scrutinise data rather than assume meanings and drive agendas.
Groupthink and the Climate Club
Appointing people who think alike manufactures groupthink. Its symptoms are obvious in climate policy. Reports recycle slogans: “climate crisis”, “sea level rise”, “unprecedented extremes”, “hottest year on record”. Critics are dismissed as “deniers” or “anti-science”. The result is an intellectual monoculture where outlandish predictions go unchallenged and policy narrows to the same prescriptions: higher targets, more subsidies, faster transitions.
Consequences for Policy and Debate
Largely due to WWF and Purves’ campaigns, Australia committed to the non-binding Paris Agreement pledging to crater the economy on the altar of net zero. To meet legislated targets will require a costly energy restructure, farmland the size of half of Victoria turned into forests, the same again covered in solar panels, and habitat-wrecking wind turbines — all with bipartisan support.
These decisions are defended as if “the science is settled” and “the experts agree”. But the science is not settled, and the experts agree only because dissent is excluded. The ABC talks to the Climate Council, journalists recycle press releases, and citizens are told there is no alternative. Leaders claim they merely follow advice. The result is a narrowing of debate. Meanwhile, costs mount, prices rise, industries go broke or move off-shore, and vast sums are channelled into projects whose benefits will never be realised.
Basic questions — about the accuracy of scenarios, of long-term temperature data, of instrument changes at weather stations, or of natural variability — are left unanswered.
Australia needs an honest conversation about the climate — not whether it changes, but about how we know what we know, who gets to speak with authority and how much of what, those people actually know. At present, a small interconnected group of activists and academics dominate the stage, presenting themselves as arbiters of truth. In reality, they are committed to a narrative, dismissive of dissent, and too close to government and NGOs to claim independence.We should demand better. A truly independent authority would include experts with diverse views from disciplines beyond the usual suspects and be required to defend conclusions against conflicting evidence. It would disclose funding and affiliations openly and recognise uncertainty, not bury it.
Until then, climate policy in Australia will remain the product of a closed conversation among like-minded insiders. As long as that remains the case, the public is entitled to ask: whose interests are really being served? Robert Purves and WWF, Tim Flannery, Leslie Hughes, Amanda McKenzie, Anna Rose, Matt Keane, and others in the Climate Club, or us — citizens, including farmers, who stand to lose their livelihoods due to climate action?
Protecting our freedoms and way of life is worth more than a passing thought.
Dr Bill Johnston publishes the results of his work at BoM Watch
